en: The Accomplishment of the Ascertainment of Wisdom and Means. First Chapter.
Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
Therein is the peerless Dharma-body of the Buddha, pure by nature and unstained by the entire mass of conceptual constructions of all beings, through the increase of the True Dharma.
And enjoyment, fashioned in various forms, arises as a well-constructed emanation.
Having prostrated to that which consists of wisdom and skillful means, this very [work] is now fully explained. ||1||
By me, the illustrious Anaṅgavajra, this has been composed in brief according to the true nature of reality for the benefit of all living beings who do not know its essential character. (2)
An entity born from unreal conceptualization consists of mere imagination;
that very existence is described by the wise as a deluder of the foolish. (3)
From that, there arise the entire mass of unbearable afflictions and,
repeatedly, a great multitude of various types of karmic actions.
And from those two, beginning with death and birth, suffering arises incessantly and in extreme abundance for those whose minds are attached and lack faith. (5)

As long as there is the great grasping at existence for those dwelling in the prison of cyclic existence, so long, due to the lack of wisdom, will there be neither their own welfare nor the welfare of others. //6//
Therefore, by the wise who desire to bring joy to the three worlds and who wish to remove their own delusion, the grasping at existence must be abandoned. (7)
Having abandoned the grasping for existence, the wise person should not imagine non-existence;
even if there were a difference between these two, the conceptual construction itself would not differ.
Indeed, the conceptualization of existence is better than the fabrication of non-existence;
for a lamp that is burning goes out, but once extinguished, what destination could it go to? (9)
As long as there is conceptualization of an entity, so long indeed is that entity perceived;
for here, there can be no destruction of space, which is devoid of a beginning. (10)
Even if it were to be established as a mere non-existence, it would still lack any means [of realization];
being incapable of accomplishing the welfare of oneself or others due to its state of non-existence, it is like a sky-flower. ||11||
Thus, existence should be relinquished because it is illusory, like a magical illusion;
and non-existence should also be relinquished by those who desire the fruit of Buddhahood, because it is a mere absence. (12)
O wise ones, now hear how, through the abandonment of these two, there is that state which is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa, and which remains as it is. (13)
Through the downward movement of thorough investigation, the lack of intrinsic nature of phenomena is realized;
that which is distinguished by the division of knowledge and the object of knowledge is called the reality of wisdom (prajñātattva). ||14||
Because one has caused all sentient beings to rise above the entire flood of suffering by removing them from its causes, compassion is therefore proclaimed as a form of attachment. (15)
That which brings about the desired object by means of favorable application, like a boat [carrying one] according to the current, is proclaimed as the "means" (upāya). ||16||
That which is the union of both, like water and milk, through the application of the non-dual form—that is called wisdom and means (prajñopāya). //17//
That in which neither addition nor subtraction is possible, and that which has been described for the sake of such addition—that is called the true nature of reality (dharmatattva). //18//
Abandoned by the grasped and the grasper, free from the mire of existence and non-existence, liberated from both the characterized and the characteristic, it is pure and naturally stainless. (19)
Neither dual nor non-dual, peaceful and auspicious, it abides everywhere;
it is to be personally realized within, immovable, and undisturbed by wisdom and means. (20)
That very [nature] is the most wonderful abode of all Buddhas;
it is proclaimed as the divine Dharmadhātu, which brings about the attainment of supreme welfare. ||21||
Non-abiding nirvāṇa, practiced by the Buddhas of the three times, the delightful state of self-consecration, auspicious through the perfection of wisdom. (22)
The three bodies, the three vehicles, and the countless millions of mantras;
the wheel of the mudrās and maṇḍalas, and that which is the unsurpassed Kaula. ||23||
All the gods, lords of the Daityas, and humans emerged from there;
likewise, the pretas and others were indeed obstructed within that darkness.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, he remains forever for the entire world, perfectly bestowing the state of enjoyment and liberation through the nature of wisdom and skillful means. (25)

Having realized this very [truth], the Buddhas, the Sugatas, attained perfect awakening in the past; they attain it everywhere now, and those who work for the welfare of the world will attain it in the future. (26)
Because its nature is infinite bliss, it is adorned with glorious great bliss;
it is the foremost Samantabhadra, which brings about perfect awakening. (27)
The equanimity of one whose sole activity is the destruction of all suffering in the three worlds, whose compassion is incomparable, whose supreme intellect is liberated from attachment,
and who possesses an immeasurable mass of diverse objects of knowledge;
The lords of sages have declared that reality is the constituent factor for the happiness of oneself, others, and both. ||28||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Wisdom and Means," from the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*.
The second chapter.
Now, therefore, something is being told for the sake of attaining the jewel of reality, for the benefit of those whose souls are deluded by the confusion of difficult-to-pierce worldly existence. (1)
This method has been concisely set forth by the former Buddhas, and by the illustrious Anaṅgavajra, whose mind was permeated with compassion. (2)
"This is that"—even for the Victors, it is impossible to describe it in such a way.
Because its nature is to be personally realized within, it is not grasped as an external object. ||3||
And likewise, it has been taught in due order by the perfectly awakened ones of the three times, who bring joy to the world, within the sūtras, tantras, practices, and so forth. (4)

That [Reality] can never indeed be attained through knowledge derived from hearing and so forth, because there is no relationship between words and their referents; it is indicated by the definition of the scripture itself. ||5||
Therefore, service to the true guru must always be practiced with devotion;
for without it, the ultimate reality is not attained even in tens of millions of eons.
But when the jewel of reality has not been attained, there is never any accomplishment whatsoever;
just as there is no sprout even in a perfectly pure and excellent field if the seed is absent. (7)

Whosoever there may be who teach the meaning of wisdom and skillful means through peaceful means, they are as wondrous as a wish-fulfilling gem, abiding on the path beyond conceptual construction. ||8||
Having thoroughly understood the teachers on this earth according to their true nature, one should serve them with diligence for the sake of attaining the supreme realization of the Self. (9)
By whose splendor the infinite bliss of a bodhisattva is attained, and the state of preeminence among all beings in the three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving. (10)
Why, then, do those of evil intent approach that embodiment of compassion, who is affectionate without cause, with minds defiled by illusion? (11)
Having firmly served the true guru with prostrations and honors that are not false,
and through offerings such as milk and worship, [one attains success] for as long as one's lifespan lasts.
But when the jewel of reality— the abode of all the qualities of a Buddha— is attained,
those who are cruel in their search for faults do not even ask for news of it.
Likewise, other evil-minded ones also approach those who carry the preceptor’s staff;
with their wicked intentions, they bring harm upon themselves by their own actions. (14)

The appropriation of the Guru’s consort and of one who upholds the Three Jewels, as well as the denial of the non-conceptual state and the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) by a yogin, are to be rejected. (15)
Thus it was spoken by the illustrious Vajranātha during the most wondrous samaya:
"Those who always harbor feelings of disgust and cause terror to their own mothers... (16)
Having previously served a single teacher, the wicked, thinking "he does not favor me," resort to another, eager to proclaim his faults. (17)
"How might we obtain the designation of 'yogin' and 'teacher'?"—driven by this alone, they do not seek after Buddhahood. (18)
Having somehow attained that knowledge, some do not respect their former teacher;
they say, "We are the knowers," while others do not even say this out of pride. (19)
And others, being enraged, said: "Take what has been offered;
I am no longer your disciple, nor are you now my teacher. (20)
How could there be success or even happiness in this life for those whose minds are intent on deceiving their gurus? They wander about, utterly deluded. (21)

And those beings who are of such a kind—those who are turned away from the accomplishment of their own welfare—all of them have been declared by the glorious Vajranātha to be vessels for the lower realms. (22)
For those who hate the knower of the Self, there is no destination other than hell;
performing terrible deeds, they are intensely cooked by manifold sufferings. (23)
Therefore, the teacher, who bestows infinite fruit, should always be served with one's whole being by the virtuous who desire their own ultimate welfare. (24)

Having abandoned envy and avarice, as well as pride and egoism, and likewise having cast aside that which is accomplished through deceit, those who have made a firm resolve for perfect enlightenment— ||25||
With a mind unshakable through conduct that is always solely for the benefit of others, one should attend upon the Lord of the World, the Guru who bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (26)
Disregarding one's own affairs, preceded by worship and the mandala, one should perform prostrations at his feet with the head three times a day with supreme devotion. ||27||
Then, by the grace of the Guru's feet, the disciples attain without obstacle the supreme reality as it has been taught by those whose intellects have realized the three paths. (28)
The bodhicitta is eternally luminous, pure, the abode of the Victors, consisting of all phenomena, divine, and the cause of the locus of everything. ||29||
Just as a sun-crystal gem blazes forth intensely and instantly through the proximity of the sun, which has destroyed the thick darkness, so too [does this occur]. (30)
Due to the proximity of the sun-like radiance of the yoga of reality, which perceives the world, the jewel-like mind of the disciple likewise blazes, its dark ignorance having been dispelled. //31//
Immediately upon awakening, the glorious one was illuminated by the lamp of the jewels of reality;
his mind was moved by the compassion of the Buddhas residing in the ten directions. (32)
Having arrived swiftly, he is certainly empowered by the Perfectly Awakened Ones;
and through the empowerment of the Buddhas, he becomes equal to all Buddhas. ||33||
Having abandoned all pride, rivalry, and the veil of deceit,
those steadfast ones who here serve the Teacher with constant practice and untiring faith have attained the foremost state of all the Sugatas,
having reached enlightenment.
Surely they shall attain that jewel of reality, the state of the qualities of the Victors. //34//
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Propitiation of the Vajrācārya," in the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*.
The third chapter.
Now, therefore, for the benefit of practitioners who seek the state of Vajrasattva, the consecration—the abode of the three realms—is correctly explained. (1)
When a wise person has been consecrated according to the path of mantra, they are in the direct presence of all the Buddhas within the mandala, the abode of the Sugatas. ||2||
Nevertheless, the Lord of infinite world-realms should be grasped by the wise one who, fearing injury to the *samaya*, has attained the stage of self-consecration. (3)
And so it has been stated by the Perfectly Awakened Ones in the Mantra Path from the perspective of ultimate truth:
"The commitment (samaya) of the deities such as Vajrasattva is difficult to transgress. (4)
Then, therefore, with every effort for the sake of consecration, the son of the Conqueror should approach, as is appropriate, the ocean of qualities that is the Vajrācārya. (5)
Having obtained a beautiful-eyed mudrā endowed with fresh youth, one should adorn her with garlands, sandalwood paste, fine garments, and so forth, and then present her.
Having diligently worshipped the Leader with devotion, using perfumes, garlands, and other honors, as well as extensive offerings such as milk, together with the mudrā; ||7||
The disciple, having placed his kneecaps upon the ground with faith, should request the scripture with palms joined in reverence and with this hymn of praise: ||8||
Salutations to you, whose essence is emptiness, who are free from all conceptual constructions;
O Omniscient One, mass of gnosis, embodiment of wisdom, homage be to you! (9)
O Vajrasattva, who severs the ignorance of the world, who teaches the meaning of the pure reality, and who has arisen from the selflessness of phenomena—homage be to you! (10)
The perfectly awakened Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the qualities of the perfections, always arise from you, O Protector; homage be to you, the thought of awakening! (11)
The Three Jewels, the Mahāyāna, and all this world of moving and unmoving beings within the triple realm—O Hero, everything originates from you; homage be to you! (12)
O wondrous one, like a wish-fulfilling gem for the accomplishment of the desired aims of the world; O glorious son of the Buddha, who carries out the command of the Sugata, homage be to you! (13)
O ocean of virtues, through your grace I have realized the unsurpassed reality;
O Omniscient One, now grant me the favor of the vajra-abhiseka. (14)
The secret of all the Buddhas has been revealed by the Holder of the Dharma-Vajra;
just as it was by the Illustrious Citta-Vajra, so may you, O Lord, be gracious to me. (15)
Having abandoned [all else] at your lotus feet, no other refuge exists for me;
therefore, O Lord of Compassion, conqueror of the path of saṃsāra, show me mercy. 16.
Then the glorious Vajrācārya, compassionate and with a benevolent intent, having aroused pity, summoned the disciple to the maṇḍala of the assembly. (17)
It was strewn with the five strands of sensual pleasure, radiant with canopies spread above,
joined by the union of yoginīs and yogas, and filled with the ringing sound of bells.
In that most wonderful abode of Vajrasattva and the other deities, which is delightful, filled with flowers and incense, and possesses the excellent bliss of the fragrance of garlands and wine. (19)
Then, having performed the yoga of the mudrā, the preceptor, most fortunate and supreme,
places the bodhicitta within the lotus-vessel, the abode of the Victors.
Then the Lord of the World should consecrate the disciple, who is joined with the mudrās, amidst raised yak-tail whisks, parasols, and auspicious songs of verses. (21)
Having bestowed the consecration with excellent jewels, the preceptor, who is the Supreme Lord,
shall indeed grant the beautiful, divine, and inherently pure *samaya*.
The great jewel together with camphor, joined with red sandalwood, combined with the water of the thunderbolt, and the fifth arising from speech. 23.
"O child, this commitment has been proclaimed for you by the Buddhas of the past; O auspicious one, always observe it. Now listen to the vow. (24)
One must not commit the slaughter of living beings; do not abandon the Three Jewels. Your teacher must not be forsaken, for the vow is difficult to transgress. (25)
Then, to that disciple who has been consecrated with the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) and is free from sin, one should grant permission, for he is the foremost son of the Buddhas. (26)
O supreme among beings, set in motion the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma in every direction, extending as far as the seat of enlightenment. (27)
Your very self, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, is said to be like a wish-fulfilling gem;
untiring and free from attachment, act now for the sake of sentient beings. (28)

Having received the consecration, being permitted by his preceptor, having accomplished his purpose, and being filled with joy, he should utter very sweet speech that brings delight to the world. (29)
Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life as well;
today I am born into the family of the Buddhas and have now become a son of the Buddha. (30)
O Lord, I have been rescued by you from the most terrible ocean of kalpas, which is agitated by the waves of birth and difficult to cross because of the mire of afflictions.
Through your grace, I know myself as if already perfected;
I have no longing for enlightenment, for all latent predispositions have been abandoned. (32)
Having prostrated at his feet with devotion, his eyes wide with joy,
he should offer whatever object is most dear to him.
Even by a compassionate teacher whose mind is free from restraint, [the teaching] should be accepted for the sake of removing the student's misconceptions and for his benefit. //34//
Then, having prostrated, performed worship, and given the teacher's fee (guru-dakṣiṇā), one who has attained the desired state should further make this request: ||35||
Now, may the foremost Buddha of existence be well-pleased toward me, so that through his grace I may accomplish unexcelled enlightenment. (36)
Having accomplished the unsurpassed state of Buddhahood, which is honored above all, I shall establish therein all sentient beings dwelling within the three realms of existence. (37)
The consecration should be bestowed according to the prescribed rites,
having understood the disciple’s inclination with one's own mind;
[the disciple] who is devoted to the noble and profound method.
One should bestow the jewel of consecration by means of speech alone. ||38||
Having attained the peerless excellence of the supreme consecration of the Vajra, which is difficult to obtain even for all those who have reached [the goal],
he performs the act of grasping the glory of the realm of enjoyment; he is the consecration of the Great Bodhicitta,
one whose intellect is prepared for the undertaking of victory over the enemies that are the evils of the three worlds, having received the permission [to proceed].
Having established the mind upon awakening, the yogi of reality should practice here with a vast and stainless mind. //39//
Thus ends the third chapter, the Consecration of Bodhicitta, in the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now, therefore, the supreme cultivation of wisdom and means is clearly explained for the benefit of practitioners who have initiated their vigor for the sake of others. (1)
Having meditated upon which, yogins do not remain in the terrible cycle of existence—a sea difficult to cross—nor do they abide even in nirvāṇa for the sake of their own self-interest alone. (2)
The unsurpassed awakening of the Buddhas, which is stainless and marvelous, has arisen as the ultimate limit of excellence, being entirely free from decrease or increase. //3//
He who does not transcend the phenomena such as the five aggregates, nor ever grasps them, [realizes] the sameness of the nature of all phenomena. (4)
One should not practice the meditation on emptiness, nor should one practice the meditation on non-emptiness;
the yogi should neither abandon emptiness nor reject non-emptiness. (5)

When there is grasping at both the empty and the non-empty, a vast proliferation of conceptualization arises; and even in the renunciation [of that grasping], there is still a mental construction. Therefore, one should abandon this dyad.
Freed from both the grasping and the abandoning [of objects], and devoid of a basis, this conceptual construction "I" [arises]; therefore, one should abandon this dyad.

The wise one should meditate [on the Self] as being changeless, unattached, free from desire, and devoid of impurity; liberated from the conceptualization of beginning and end, it is like the sky. ||8||
A compassionate person should not turn away from sentient beings;
nor should they conceptualize whether a so-called "sentient being" exists or does not exist.
Because its essential nature is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it is celebrated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Compassion is like a wish-fulfilling gem, accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings without exception. //10//
In the state of non-referentiality, wisdom is non-referential and great compassion is non-referential;
they become one with the intellect, like space merging with space. (11)
There is no meditator whatsoever, nor is there any meditation;
there is nothing at all to be meditated upon—this is called the meditation on reality. //12//
There is no agent here whatsoever, nor is there any enjoyer found;
the realization of the ultimate truth is entirely free from both agent and enjoyer. 13.
And herein there is no grasper whatsoever, nor is there anyone who presents [an object];
therefore, there is nothing to be abandoned, and no object of grasping exists here at all. (14)
While seeing all forms, hearing sounds, speaking, laughing, or even eating various flavors. (15)
For those yogis who know reality and whose minds have gone elsewhere while performing all their duties, yoga arises incessantly. (16)
This is called non-duality; it is the supreme bodhicitta, the Vajra, the glorious Vajrasattva, the perfectly awakened Buddha, and awakening itself. (17)
And this perfection of wisdom consists of all the perfections;
it is said to be this very equanimity, the supreme cultivation of all the Buddhas. (18)
Right here, this entire world, consisting of the stable and the moving, has arisen;
as well as the infinite bodhisattvas, the perfectly awakened buddhas, the śrāvakas, and so forth. (19)

The yogi should meditate on that very [reality] by way of being free from existence and non-existence; one who meditates while liberated from both existence and non-existence attains success quickly. (20)
Hating all faults without exception and turning away from afflictions, he will certainly possess infinite, glorious, and auspicious qualities of a Sugata. (21)
Overwhelmed by the darkness of manifold conceptualizations, flickering like lightning driven by a tempestuous wind, and smeared with the stains of passion and other unrestrainable defilements—
For the Vajra-holder declared that the mind is indeed saṃsāra. ||22||
Luminous, liberated from conceptual construction, with the stains of passion and other defilements abandoned—
O Supreme Being, it is neither the grasped nor the grasper.
He declared that very thing to be the supreme nirvāṇa. ||23||
And therefore, there is nothing beyond this that serves as the cause for the great mass of suffering; rather,
it is the cause for the arising of infinite happiness.
For those seeking liberation, there is nothing beyond that. ||24||

Those who have girded their loins for the destruction of all suffering without exception and who desire to attain the true bliss of perfect enlightenment should steady the mind and investigate with diligence.
Let its intrinsic nature be made into an intrinsic nature. ||25||
As long as the minds of living beings are obstructed by the heavy veil of the darkness of conceptual construction (kalpatamaḥ), so long will there be endless suffering;
once they are freed from that, there will be sublime and incomparable happiness. Therefore, the Noble Ones should apply themselves with earnest intent to this.
For the sake of accomplishing that task, they themselves protect their vast association with him. ||26||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Cultivation of Reality," in the *Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi*.
